extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS authors, reviewers, program chairs, and the machine-learning research community interested in peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Summaries and experimental results about NeurIPS 2021 peer-review processes, including a duplicated-paper consistency experiment and an author-perception survey; documents metrics, definitions, findings, and procedural details used to evaluate conference review consistency and author calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicated-papers experiment design
rubrics_metrics.description: During assignment, 10% of papers were chosen uniformly at random as ‘duplicated papers’; each duplicated paper was copied and two independent committees (ACs and twice the normal number of reviewers) were assigned to the two copies, with the two ACs assigned to different SACs, reviewers conflicted across copies, and committees not told about the experiment. Authors of duplicated papers were notified right before initial reviews were released and asked to respond to each set of reviews independently and to keep the experiment confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the exact procedural setup for measuring decision consistency: random selection fraction (10%), assignment rules (two ACs, double reviewers), SAC separation, conflict handling, and author notification timing. It also notes that newly invited reviewers for one copy were made conflicts for the other copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rule for duplicated papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicated papers were accepted if at least one of the two copies was recommended for acceptance and no 'fatal flaw' was found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This acceptance decision rule affects outcome counts and interpretation of inconsistency: some papers were accepted only because one committee recommended acceptance; the rule produced cases accepted that otherwise might not have been.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inconsistent outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The fraction of duplicated papers that were accepted by only one of the two committees (as either a poster, a spotlight, or an oral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the principal metric of decision inconsistency; reported as 203 out of 882 = 23.0% in 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-baseline comparison for inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute expected fraction of inconsistent outcomes under a random model where each committee accepts a paper independently with probability p (the acceptance rate); compare observed inconsistency to this baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides context: e.g., for p = 0.227 the random baseline disagreement is 35.1%; observed disagreement can be expressed as a relative improvement over the random baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bump-status-adjusted inconsistency (alternative definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain paired labels are not considered inconsistent—specifically treating 'Accept that can be bumped down' vs 'Reject', and 'Reject that can be bumped up' vs 'Poster Accept that shouldn't be bumped up to Spotlight'—the measured fraction of inconsistent outcomes drops (in the report, to 16%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alternative counting recognizes calibration/bump metadata in meta-reviews and produces a lower inconsistency estimate by ignoring cases that committees explicitly flagged as near-boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept precision / arbitrariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept precision (and its complement called 'arbitrariness') measured as the fraction of papers accepted by one committee that would be rejected by a re-review (i.e., accepted by first committee but rejected by second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported values: 2014 ~49.5% of first-accepted were rejected by second; 2021 was 50.6%. This quantifies how many accepted papers are not robust to re-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability a rejected paper would be accepted on re-review
rubrics_metrics.description: Metric: the fraction of rejected papers that would have been accepted if re-reviewed (reported as 14.9% in 2021, 17.5% in 2014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complements accept-precision/arbitrariness to quantify reversals in the other direction (reject → accept).

rubrics_metrics.name: High-tier selection disagreement metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of disagreement specifically for orals and spotlights: count of spotlights/orals recommended by one committee but rejected by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed especially high disagreement for orals/spotlights; example: more than half of all spotlights recommended by either committee were rejected by the other (13/25 and 13/23). This highlights instability at the top of the selection hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal-rate post-review
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the rate at which authors withdraw papers after initial reviews are released; comparison between duplicated and non-duplicated papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported that withdrawal rate after seeing initial reviews was 45% higher for papers not in the experiment compared with duplicated papers (authors of duplicated papers had two shots at acceptance). Authors were most likely to withdraw if both copies were headed for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: AC/SAC feedback categories for causes of disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad categories reported by ACs/SACs explaining why committees disagreed: (1) 'noise on the decision frontier' — borderline cases with no real disagreement, (2) genuine disagreement about contribution value or severity of limitations, (3) one committee found a significant issue (e.g., close prior work, incorrect proofs, methodological flaws) that the other did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey feedback: 48% labeled as borderline/noise, 45% 'I still stand by our committee’s decision', 7% 'I believe the other committee made the right decision'. This classification helps diagnose sources of inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-response-asymmetric-effort confound
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: some authors spent significantly more effort responding to the copy they believed was more likely to be accepted, including 50 pairs where authors only left comments on the higher-scored copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavioural confound may bias acceptance rates for duplicated papers and explains part of the observed differences between duplicated and non-duplicated paper acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review editing / calibration confound
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation: during calibration, ACs sometimes edited meta-review decision labels (e.g., moving poster→reject) without updating bump-up/bump-down fields, producing inconsistent or nonsensical metadata and potential inaccuracies in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational issue can introduce minor inaccuracies into analyses that depend on bump-status fields or the chronology of label edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of selectivity vs arbitrariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding/recommendation: being significantly more selective (lower acceptance rate) will substantially increase arbitrariness (fraction of accepted papers that would change under re-review); increasing acceptance rate may not appreciably decrease arbitrariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as guidance for program chairs when choosing selectivity threshold; visualized by computing inconsistency under shifted acceptance thresholds (e.g., accept only orals/spotlights yields much higher disagreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Q1 — author-estimated acceptance probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey question asked at time of paper submission: 'What is your best estimate of the probability (as a percentage) that this submission will be accepted?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to measure author calibration; authors were informed of historical acceptance rates before answering. Authors substantially overestimated — median prediction 70% vs actual ~25.8%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q2 — author ranking of their submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey question (for authors with two or more papers): 'Rank your submissions in terms of your own perception of their scientific contributions to the NeurIPS community, if published in their current form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare internal perceived quality ranking vs predicted acceptance probabilities and vs actual outcomes; strict ranking agreement with Q1 predictions was 93%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q3 — change in author perception after reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey question asked after preliminary reviews: 'After you read the reviews of this paper, how did your perception of the value of its scientific contribution to the NeurIPS community change (assuming it was published in its initially submitted form)?' with choices: much more positive (++), slightly more positive (+), did not change (0), slightly more negative (-), much more negative (–).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to measure impact of reviews on author perceptions; about 50% of authors reported a change, and over 30% reported becoming more positive, both among accepted and rejected papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration metric: Brier score (squared loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibration error across sub-groups measured in terms of the Brier score (squared loss), controlling for confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables quantitative comparisons of calibration across demographic or role-based subgroups (e.g., gender, seniority, invited reviewers). Reported findings: female authors slightly worse calibration error than male authors; miscalibration decreases with seniority; invited reviewers better calibrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement between authors' perceived contribution and predicted acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metric of concordance between Q2 ranking (perceived scientific contribution) and strict ranking induced by Q1 predicted acceptance probabilities; reported 93% agreement, with 7% cases where authors predicted peer review would reject the better paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that authors' internal quality rankings largely match their acceptance-probability estimates, but nontrivial exceptions exist where authors expect review to fail to select their stronger submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-author disagreement on relative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical metric: disagreement rate between co-authors about relative scientific contribution of joint papers (for overlapping-authorship pairs where both provided rankings), about one-third of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows that substantial disagreement exists not only between reviewers but also among co-authors, suggesting intrinsic noisiness or subjectivity in assessing paper quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: recalibrate expectations and interpret outcomes cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance: because authors vastly overestimate acceptance chances and there is substantial disagreement/noise in review judgments, conference organizers and mentors should attempt to recalibrate authors' expectations and interpret acceptance/rejection outcomes with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A community-level suggestion informed by observed overprediction and inconsistency; framed as encouragement for policy discussion and mentoring practice.
